meta.source_system: Sliding puzzle / n-puzzle family (15 puzzle; Klotski is the sliding-block cognate; rules public), transcribed as the 2x3 deterministic variant: 5 numbered tiles + 1 open position, 4 slide directions, no randomness collected, no score
meta.source_citation: Wikipedia "15 puzzle" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15_puzzle): lead ("Tiles in the same row or column of the open position can be moved by sliding them horizontally or vertically, respectively."; "The goal of the puzzle is to place the tiles in numerical order (from left to right, top to bottom)."; "the 8 puzzle, which has 8 tiles in a 3x3 frame"), Solvability section ("Johnson & Story (1879) used a parity argument to show that half of the starting positions for the n puzzle are impossible to resolve"; "on boards of size m x n, where m and n are both larger than or equal to 2, all even permutations are solvable"); Wikipedia "Sliding puzzle" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sliding_puzzle): lead ("a combination puzzle that challenges a player to slide (frequently flat) pieces along certain routes (usually on a board) to establish a certain end-configuration"; "a sliding block puzzle prohibits lifting any pieces off the board"), with Klotski listed among the examples of sliding puzzles. Per-rule citations in meta.rules_with_citations; per-edge generating rules in meta.edge_rule_tags.
meta.state_encoding: state = 10 bits = the lexicographic rank of the configuration among the 6! = 720 permutations of (0..5); cells 0..5 row-major (0=top-left ... 5=bottom-right), tile value 0 = the open position, 1..5 = the numbered tiles; ranks 720..1023 are unused encoding space = 304 padding states (every action self-loops, reward 0 -- same padding convention as tcp/dhcp/imap/mini2048); a slide never produces an unused rank, so real states only reach real states
meta.semantics_class: direction-key: the four actions are slide directions bound to board coordinates (a tile slides in the named direction); a board symmetry renames the directions with the cells, so true board symmetries are explicit-caliber claims with per-element direction renamings; the fixed reading (directions pinned) is the naive contrast
meta.reward_rule: all zero by design: the puzzle has no score (see meta.rules_with_citations R4); the win condition is recorded in meta.win_condition, not as a per-edge reward (same all-zero convention as tcp/dhcp/imap/lightsout3)
meta.win_condition: tiles in numerical order from left to right, top to bottom, open position last (bottom-right): the arrangement (1,2,3,4,5,0), state index 153 -- 'The goal of the puzzle is to place the tiles in numerical order (from left to right, top to bottom)' (Wikipedia 15 puzzle lead); the puzzle does not lock on the goal, so it is an ordinary state of the transition system and goals=[] in this model

rules_with_citations.rule: one move = one numbered tile slides one grid step into the adjacent open position (the open position moves one step in the opposite direction); a tile is eligible when it sits in the same row or column as the open position and adjacent to it -- the four slide directions are the four actions
rules_with_citations.citation: Wikipedia "15 puzzle" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15_puzzle), 'Tiles in the same row or column of the open position can be moved by sliding them horizontally or vertically, respectively.' (the eligible tiles are the ones aligned with the open position; one move slides the adjacent one one step -- multi-tile push shorthands are not collected); Wikipedia "Sliding puzzle" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sliding_puzzle), 'a combination puzzle that challenges a player to slide (frequently flat) pieces along certain routes (usually on a board) to establish a certain end-configuration.'

rules_with_citations.rule: pieces never leave the board and never jump: only the tile orthogonally adjacent to the open position can slide, and a direction with no tile to slide changes nothing (the move is unavailable; recorded as a no-op self-loop with reward 0, same convention as mini2048's unavailable-direction self-loops)
rules_with_citations.citation: Wikipedia "Sliding puzzle" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sliding_puzzle), 'Unlike tour puzzles, a sliding block puzzle prohibits lifting any pieces off the board.'; the one-step adjacency follows from R1's 'the open position' wording (only the adjacent tile can slide into it in a single move)

rules_with_citations.rule: the goal configuration is the tiles in numerical order from left to right, top to bottom, with the open position last (bottom-right): the arrangement (1,2,3,4,5,0) -- recorded in meta.win_condition as a goal property
rules_with_citations.citation: Wikipedia "15 puzzle" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15_puzzle), 'The goal of the puzzle is to place the tiles in numerical order (from left to right, top to bottom).'

rules_with_citations.rule: the puzzle has no score; the reward layer is all zero by design and the win condition is recorded in meta.win_condition, not as a per-edge reward
rules_with_citations.citation: Wikipedia "15 puzzle" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15_puzzle), the article defines the goal as a configuration (R3) and describes no scoring; its solver content ('Commonly used heuristics for this problem include counting the number of misplaced tiles and finding the sum of the taxicab distances between each block and its position in the goal configuration') is solver advice, not a game payoff -- recorded, not turned into a reward; same all-zero reward convention as the tcp/dhcp/imap/lightsout3 cases

rules_with_citations.rule: RECORDED, NOT REPAIRED: moves partition the 6! = 720 configurations into two parity classes of 360 each (only half of the starting positions are solvable from a given goal); the model transcribes the FULL 720-configuration transition system -- both classes are real states and the class split is a property of the state space, machine-asserted by a BFS from the goal (360 reachable), not encoded as unreachable padding
rules_with_citations.citation: Wikipedia "15 puzzle" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15_puzzle), 'Johnson & Story (1879) used a parity argument to show that half of the starting positions for the n puzzle are impossible to resolve, no matter how many moves are made.'; 'on boards of size m x n, where m and n are both larger than or equal to 2, all even permutations are solvable'

rules_with_citations.rule: VARIANT BOUNDARY: this case is the 2x3 board (5 tiles + open position); the canonical n-puzzle is the 4x4 fifteen puzzle, the 8 puzzle plays the same rules on 3x3
rules_with_citations.citation: Wikipedia "15 puzzle" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15_puzzle), 'It has 15 square tiles numbered 1 to 15 in a frame that is 4 tile positions high and 4 tile positions wide, with one unoccupied position.'; 'Similar names are used for different sized variants of the 15 puzzle, such as the 8 puzzle, which has 8 tiles in a 3x3 frame.'; the m x n family with m, n >= 2 is covered by the Johnson & Story solvability theorem quoted in R5; Klotski (listed among the examples of sliding puzzles) is the sliding-block cognate of this family

rules_with_citations.rule: play itself is deterministic: a slide always moves exactly the one adjacent tile, with no randomness; the physical puzzle's initial scramble is the only stochastic step and it is NOT collected (outside the deterministic FSM semantics)
rules_with_citations.citation: consequence of R1 as stated by Wikipedia "Sliding puzzle" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sliding_puzzle), and Wikipedia "15 puzzle" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15_puzzle),  (a slide moves exactly one tile; nothing else happens); same not-collected discipline as mini2048's random-spawn rule

rules_with_citations.rule: family placement: the numbered uniform-tile n-puzzle member of the sliding-puzzle family; Klotski is the unequal-block cognate and is NOT transcribed here (its multi-cell pieces would need a different state space)
rules_with_citations.citation: Wikipedia "Sliding puzzle" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sliding_puzzle), 'A sliding puzzle, sliding block puzzle, or sliding tile puzzle is a combination puzzle ...' with 'Fifteen puzzle' and 'Klotski' listed among its examples of sliding puzzles; Wikipedia "15 puzzle" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15_puzzle), for the numbered uniform-tile member

edge_rule_tags.layout: edge_rule_tags.values[s] is a 4-character string, character a in {S,I,P} = the generating rule of edge (s, action a); S=a tile slid into the open position (R1), I=no tile to slide in this direction (no-op self-loop, R2), P=padding self-loop. Every real edge of this model is generated by R1 (the slide) or is an R2 unavailable-direction no-op; the 304 padding states self-loop on all four actions (P)

transcription_notes: scope: 2x3 board, 5 numbered tiles + 1 open position, 4 slide directions; the deterministic slide mechanics of the n-puzzle family (rule R1) with the initial scramble NOT collected (rule R7) -- randomness is not part of the deterministic FSM semantics, per the court's not-collected discipline (same pattern as mini2048's random-spawn rule).

VARIANT BOUNDARY (rule R6): the 2x3 board; the canonical n-puzzle is the 4x4 fifteen puzzle and the 8 puzzle plays on 3x3 ('Similar names are used for different sized variants of the 15 puzzle, such as the 8 puzzle, which has 8 tiles in a 3x3 frame', Wikipedia). Every cited rule sentence is size-independent except the board size; the m x n family with m, n >= 2 is covered by Johnson & Story's solvability theorem; Klotski is the sliding-block cognate, not transcribed here.

actions: four slide directions indexed 0=up, 1=down, 2=left, 3=right; the direction names the motion of the sliding TILE (a tile slides in that direction into the adjacent open position), so the open position moves one step in the opposite direction. The source names no action numbering; the indices are this transcription's own convention, recorded here and in meta.action_names.

encoding: state = 10 bits = the lexicographic rank of the configuration among the 6! = 720 permutations of (0..5) (cells 0..5 row-major; value 0 = the open position, 1..5 = the numbered tiles). Ranks 720..1023 are unused encoding space: 304 padding states, every action self-loops with reward 0 (same padding convention as tcp/dhcp/imap/mini2048). Real states only reach real states: a slide rearranges tiles, and a rearrangement of (0..5) is again a permutation of (0..5), so a slide never produces an unused rank (machine-asserted by this generator on every run).

parity recorded, not repaired (rule R5): the 720 real states split into two move-invariant classes of 360 each (Johnson & Story 1879); both classes are real states of this model. BFS from the goal configuration reaches exactly 360 of them (machine-asserted on every run); the other 360 are the unsolvable-from-goal class, present and well-formed.

rewards: all zero by design (rule R4) -- the puzzle has no score; the win condition (tiles in numerical order, open position last: arrangement (1,2,3,4,5,0)) is recorded in meta.win_condition as a goal property and the puzzle does not lock on it, so it is an ordinary state of the transition system and goals=[] in this model. The adjudication therefore runs entirely on the transition layer (same all-zero convention as tcp/dhcp/imap/lightsout3).

explicit caliber note: a board symmetry renames the slide directions element-by-element (mirroring the board left-right turns 'a tile slides left' into 'a tile slides right'); rho(identity)=id while rho(hflip)!=id, so no single action_map can serve a whole closed group. Since 2026-11-04 the engine's group format accepts semantics.action_maps (one bijection per element, parallel to elements, homomorphism-law checked at load); each explicit group file here declares the per-element maps of its own elements, and meta.per_element_action_maps holds the full derivation (exhaustively derived over all 4! = 24 direction permutations, unique per element, asserted on every run).

why V4: the 2x3 board is a non-square rectangle, so its geometric symmetry group is the Klein four-group V4 = C2 x C2 of order 4 (identity, left-right mirror, top-bottom mirror, 180-degree rotation) -- no 90-degree rotation exists. The generator enumerates all 720 cell bijections against the 2x3 adjacency graph and machine-asserts exactly 4 survivors (the V4 content maps): a third group structure on the docket, distinct from mini2048's and lightsout3's D4 (order 8) and lightsout3's D4 x C2 (order 16).

padding positive control: 304 real padding states exist (the unused ranks), so the pads swap of mini2048's g6 returns here as g3_pads after lightsout3's pads-less docket entry (lightsout3 has no padding states at all; its deviation note, ruled 2026-11-04: faithful transcription outranks control-form symmetry, is the honest record of that gap). Placement note: mini2048 pairs the explicit caliber with real padding states and a pads control on the same docket; this case pairs them again on a third group structure (V4).
